citation: Heissel JA, Norris S. Rise and Shine: The Effect of School Start Times on Academic Performance from Childhood through Puberty. Journal of Human Resources. 2018;53(4):957-992.
target_unit: SD of FCAT reading score per hour later start relative to sunrise
your_quote: In reading, an extra hour of sunlight before school increases scores by 0.057 SDs for adolescents and 0.061 SDs younger children. ... [Table 4, col. (3) Reading score (in SD)] Start time - sunrise (h) (pubescent) 0.057** / (0.023) ... Number of students 25,191 / Observations 104,791
your_note: Working-paper/published text of Heissel & Norris (2018) retrieved as PDF (main text + appendix) and converted with pdftotext. Value taken directly, no conversion: reading score in SD units per +1 h of start time relative to sunrise, adolescent (pubescent) group. SE 0.023 is the clustered (individual-level) standard error printed under the coefficient in Table 4 column (3), the specification whose point estimate (0.057) the abstract and conclusion quote for adolescent reading. n = 25,191 students (104,791 student-year observations). Identification is a 2SLS/IV design: cross-time-zone moves instrument for sunlight before school, with the start-time x puberty interaction also instrumented; I classed this as instrumental_variable / T2 rather than quasi_experiment. Ambiguity: several other tables give adolescent reading coefficients of 0.048-0.061 depending on specification (Table 3: 0.061*, Table 5: 0.060**), so an extractor using a different preferred column could plausibly report 0.048-0.061.

citation: Itani O, Jike M, Watanabe N, Kaneita Y. Short sleep duration and health outcomes: a systematic review, meta-analysis, and meta-regression. Sleep Med. 2017 Apr;32:246-256.
your_quote: Similar significant results were observed in diabetes mellitus (1.37, 1.22-1.53), hypertension (1.17, 1.09-1.26), cardiovascular diseases (1.16, 1.10-1.23), coronary heart diseases (1.26, 1.15-1.38), and obesity (1.38, 1.25-1.53).
your_note: Only the PubMed abstract was retrievable (ScienceDirect returned 403; no PMC deposit). Conversion: RR 1.17 -> log_rr = ln(1.17) = 0.157004; SE = (ln(1.26) - ln(1.09))/3.92 = (0.231112 - 0.086178)/3.92 = 0.036973. Positive = elevated hypertension risk with short sleep, matching the required sign convention. your_n is null: the paper's cumulative total of 5,172,710 participants across 153 studies is for all outcomes pooled, and the hypertension-specific number of participants/datasets is only in the full text/supplement, which I could not obtain, so I did not want to attribute the all-outcome total to this estimate. Constituent studies are prospective cohorts with self-reported baseline sleep, hence T5; RoB moderate for residual confounding and exposure misclassification inherent to self-reported sleep in cohorts.

citation: Danielsson K, Markström A, Broman JE, von Knorring L, Jansson-Fröjmark M. Delayed sleep phase disorder in a Swedish cohort of adolescents and young adults: Prevalence and associated factors. Chronobiol Int. 2016;33(10):1331-1339.
your_quote: DSP occurred at a frequency of 4.6% and DSPD at a frequency of 4% in the investigated cohort.
your_note: Only the PubMed abstract was retrievable (Taylor & Francis full text not accessible). The target construct is the delayed sleep phase TRAIT without the disorder, which maps to the paper's 'DSP' category (DSPD, the disorder, is reported separately at 4%): value = 0.046 as a proportion. n = 680 derived arithmetically: questionnaire sent to 1000 randomly selected 16-26 year olds with a 68% response rate, 1000 x 0.68 = 680. SE derived as a binomial SE: sqrt(0.046 x 0.954 / 680) = sqrt(0.00006454) = 0.008033; the paper reports no CI or SE for the prevalence. Confidence medium because I could not confirm from the full text that the DSP and DSPD groups are mutually exclusive (the abstract's framing implies they are, i.e. 4.6% DSP without disorder plus 4% DSPD), nor confirm the exact analytic denominator after item non-response. RoB na: descriptive prevalence, not an exposure-outcome contrast.

citation: Hasin DS, Sarvet AL, Meyers JL, Saha TD, Ruan WJ, Stohl M, Grant BF. Epidemiology of Adult DSM-5 Major Depressive Disorder and Its Specifiers in the United States. JAMA Psychiatry. 2018;75(4):336-346.
target_unit: 12-month prevalence of DSM-5 MDD, US males aged 18+
your_quote: Male | 7.2 (0.26) | 0.5 (0.46-0.55) | 14.7 (0.40) | 0.5 (0.46-0.53) [Table 1. Prevalence and OR of 12-Month and Lifetime DSM-5 MDD by Sociodemographic Characteristics; 12-mo MDD Prevalence, % (SE)]
your_note: Full text obtained via PMC. The 12-month prevalence of DSM-5 MDD among US men is 7.2% with a survey-design SE of 0.26 percentage points; converted to the probability scale: value = 0.072, SE = 0.0026. Corroborating narrative: 'The respective 12-month and lifetime prevalences were 13.4% and 26.1% among women and 7.2% and 14.7% among men.' your_n is null: the NESARC-III total analytic sample is 36,309 adults (3,963 with 12-month MDD) but the male-only denominator is not reported in the paper, and quoting 36,309 would overstate the sample for a male-specific estimate. RoB na: weighted descriptive prevalence from a national probability survey.

citation: Qiu-Qiang Z, Wei-Wei Y, Shan-Shu H, Yi-Ran L. Mendelian randomization of individual sleep traits associated with major depressive disorder. J Affect Disord. 2024 Nov 15;365:105-111.
your_quote: A significant causal relationship between insomnia and increased risk of MDD was observed (OR: 1.233; 95 % CI: 1.214-1.253, P<0.001).
your_note: Only the PubMed abstract was retrievable (ScienceDirect returned 403). Target construct 'mdd_from_insomnia' maps to the insomnia -> MDD IVW estimate, not to the short-sleep-duration estimate (which is OR 1.179, 1.108-1.255) or the continuous sleep-duration estimate (OR 0.998). Conversion: log_or = ln(1.233) = 0.209450; SE = (ln(1.253) - ln(1.214))/3.92 = (0.225543 - 0.193925)/3.92 = 0.008066. Positive = elevated MDD risk with insomnia. your_n is null: MR two-sample GWAS sample sizes for the insomnia exposure and MDD outcome are only in the inaccessible full text. Note the target labels target_exposure_type 'other' - the exposure here is insomnia, not short sleep duration, so this estimate is only indirectly about sleep duration.

citation: Cappuccio FP, Taggart FM, Kandala NB, Currie A, Peile E, Stranges S, Miller MA. Meta-analysis of short sleep duration and obesity in children and adults. Sleep. 2008;31(5):619-626.
your_quote: Figure 4 shows the forest plot of 22 population samples from 17 observational studies of short sleep and obesity involving 603,519 adults studied around the world. Seventeen population samples showed a significant association between short duration of sleep and obesity. The pooled OR was 1.55 (1.43 to 1.68). There was no evidence of publication bias (Begg's test P = 0.09) (Figure 3b). The heterogeneity test was significant (Q = 64.0, df = 21, P < 0.001).
your_note: Full text obtained via PMC. Adult (not child) dichotomous obesity outcome: OR 1.55 (1.43-1.68). Conversion: log_or = ln(1.55) = 0.438255; SE = (ln(1.68) - ln(1.43))/3.92 = (0.518794 - 0.357674)/3.92 = 0.041102. Positive = higher obesity odds in short sleepers. n = 603,519 adults in the 22 samples contributing to the OR analysis; note the abstract instead reports 604,509 adults for the whole adult review, a small internal inconsistency in the paper. Tier TX and RoB high because the pooled adult samples are cross-sectional and the authors state 'Causal inference is difficult due to lack of control for important confounders and inconsistent evidence of temporal sequence in prospective studies'; significant heterogeneity (Q = 64.0, df = 21, P < 0.001).

citation: Brandenberger G, Weibel L. The 24-h growth hormone rhythm in men: sleep and circadian influences questioned. J Sleep Res. 2004;13(3):251-255.
your_quote: In day-active subjects, melatonin and GH showed the well-known 24-h profiles, with a major sleep-related GH pulse accounting for 52.8 +/- 3.5% of the 24-h GH production and the onset of the melatonin surge occurring at 21:53 hours +/- 18 min.
your_note: Only the PubMed abstract was retrievable (Wiley returned 403 for the J Sleep Res full text). Value 52.8 (% of 24-h GH production attributable to the sleep-related pulse) is for the ten day-active subjects sleeping 23:00-07:00 (matching target_exposure_dose_h = 8), not the eleven night workers. AMBIGUITY affecting SE: the abstract writes '52.8 +/- 3.5%' without stating whether the dispersion is SEM or SD. I entered 3.5 on the assumption it is the SEM, which is this group's usual convention for 24-h hormone profile means; if it is instead an SD, the SE would be 3.5/sqrt(10) = 1.107. This single decision is the most likely source of disagreement on this row. RoB na: descriptive endocrine measurement, no exposure contrast.

citation: Campbell IG, Burright CS, Kraus AM, Grimm KJ, Feinberg I. Daytime Sleepiness Increases With Age in Early Adolescence: A Sleep Restriction Dose-Response Study. Sleep. 2017;40(5):zsx046.
target_unit: KSS points (9-point Karolinska Sleepiness Scale) per additional hour of TIB
your_quote: Linear mixed effects analysis estimated that for the third lab visit at 15:00, the average KSS rating for 7-h TIB was 6.33 (±0.28 SE) points and decreased by 0.56 (=/− 0.07) points for each additional hour in bed.
your_note: Full text obtained via PMC. Value taken directly from the mixed-effects slope, no conversion: KSS changes by -0.56 points (SE 0.07) per ADDITIONAL hour of time in bed, i.e. sleepiness falls as TIB rises. SIGN AMBIGUITY that could easily produce disagreement: target_unit says 'per additional hour of TIB', which gives -0.56 (the paper's own sign), but target_exposure_type is 'per_hour_less_sleep' with dose 7 h vs referent 10 h, which would instead call for +0.56 (KSS rises 0.56 points per hour of sleep LOST). I followed target_unit. n = 77 children, each completing all three TIB conditions (7, 8.5, 10 h for 4 nights). Design is a within-subject lab TIB manipulation; RoB some_concerns because condition order was not randomized (the authors state it 'was not randomized but was accounted for in all statistical analyses').

citation: Marino C, Andrade B, Campisi SC, Wong M, Zhao H, Jing X, Aitken M, Bonato S, Haltigan J, Wang W, Szatmari P. Association Between Disturbed Sleep and Depression in Children and Youths: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Cohort Studies. JAMA Netw Open. 2021 Mar 1;4(3):e212373.
your_quote: The pooled OR estimate of depression in those with vs without disturbed sleep was 1.50 (95% CI, 1.13-2.00; P = .005; n = 13 006; I2 = 87.7%; P < .001) (Figure 4).
your_note: Full text obtained via PMC. Dichotomous incident-depression outcome (as opposed to the continuous depression-symptom outcome reported elsewhere in the paper): OR 1.50 (1.13-2.00). Conversion: log_or = ln(1.50) = 0.405465; SE = (ln(2.00) - ln(1.13))/3.92 = (0.693147 - 0.122218)/3.92 = 0.145645. Positive = higher odds of incident depression with disturbed sleep. n = 13,006 as printed with the pooled estimate in Results; note the Discussion says 'The meta-analytic OR in our study was based on 8 studies representing 15 438 participants', an internal inconsistency in the paper, so an extractor could reasonably enter 15,438. Exposure is 'disturbed sleep' (insomnia symptoms / sleep disturbance), not short sleep duration, consistent with target_exposure_type 'other'. Constituent studies are prospective cohorts of children/youth with questionnaire-based sleep, hence T5; RoB moderate given I2 = 87.7% and the authors' GRADE rating of 'very low' for the overall body of evidence.

citation: Hartescu I, Stensel DJ, Thackray AE, King JA, Dorling JL, Rogers EN, Sherry AP, Davies MJ, Yates T, Morgan K. Sleep extension and metabolic health in male overweight/obese short sleepers: a randomised controlled trial. J Sleep Res. 2022 Apr;31(2):e13469.
target_unit: minutes of additional actigraphic total sleep time per night at 6 weeks
your_quote: There was a significant effect of the sleep extension intervention on total sleep time change from baseline to post-intervention, with the intervention group extending their sleep by an average of 72.19 minutes/night (95% CI 57.77, 86.62 minutes/night) compared to the control group.
your_note: The Wiley full text was not accessible; I retrieved the accepted-manuscript DOCX from the authors' institutional repository (figshare) and converted it to text. Value = the ITT adjusted BETWEEN-GROUP difference in 6-week change in actigraphic TST: 72.19 min/night (95% CI 57.77, 86.62). SE = (86.62 - 57.77)/3.92 = 28.85/3.92 = 7.359694. AMBIGUITY: the published abstract instead reports the WITHIN-GROUP change in the extension arm, '79 (95% CI 68.90, 88.05) versus 6 (95% CI -4.43, 16.99) min', which would give value 79 and SE (88.05 - 68.90)/3.92 = 4.885. I chose the between-group contrast because the construct is the sleep gained FROM the programme, i.e. the randomized effect; an extractor using the abstract would enter 79. n = 18 randomized (10 extension, 8 control). RoB some_concerns: very small single-sex sample, no participant blinding possible for a behavioural sleep intervention.

citation: Dama MH, Martin J, Tassone VK, Lin Q, Lou W, Bhat V. The Association Between Delayed Sleep-Wake Phase Disorder and Depression Among Young Individuals: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Can J Psychiatry. 2025;70(12):869-886.
target_unit: SD units of depression symptom severity
your_quote: Two studies were suspected to largely contribute to the heterogeneity in the model, since both of them used predefined cut-off values for their depression measures to exclude participants from their study samples.24,46 As a part of a sensitivity analysis, we removed these two studies from the model. DSWPD status continued to have a significantly large effect on depression severity but now without any heterogeneity in the model (N: 14 estimates, 612 participants (DSWPD: 327 participants; non-DSWPD: 285 participants), Cohen's d = 1.02, 95% CI [0.85-1.19], I2 = 0%) (Figure 3(a)).
your_note: Full text obtained via PMC. The target construct (sensitivity analysis excluding the range-restricted studies) matches the primary-model sensitivity analysis: d = 1.02, 95% CI [0.85, 1.19], 14 estimates, 612 participants. SE = (1.19 - 0.85)/3.92 = 0.34/3.92 = 0.086735. SIGN: the paper reports +1.02 with higher scores meaning MORE severe depression in the DSWPD group. Per the task's convention (negative = worse outcome in the adverse-sleep condition) I flipped the sign to -1.02; an extractor reporting the paper's raw sign would enter +1.02, which is the most likely source of disagreement here. A SECOND CANDIDATE exists: the same exclusion applied to the psychiatric-disorder-controlled subgroup model gives d = 1.01, 95% CI [0.81, 1.20], 10 estimates, 454 participants; I chose the main-model version because the target does not mention the psychiatric-control restriction. Constituent comparisons are DSWPD vs non-DSWPD group differences (cross-sectional/case-control), hence TX; target_exposure_type 'descriptive' understates that this is a group contrast.

citation: Saint-Maurice PF, Freeman JR, Russ D, Almeida JS, Shams-White MM, Patel S, Wolff-Hughes DL, Watts EL, Loftfield E, Hong HG, Moore SC, Matthews CE. Associations between actigraphy-measured sleep duration, continuity, and timing with mortality in the UK Biobank. Sleep. 2024 Mar 11;47(3):zsad312.
your_quote: For example, when compared to sleep durations of 7.0 hrs/d, durations of 5 hrs/d were associated with a 29% higher risk for all-cause mortality (HR: 1.29 [1.09, 1.52]).
your_note: Full text obtained via PMC. Exposure contrast matches the target exactly (5 h/d vs 7.0 h/d referent, 7 days of wrist actigraphy). Conversion: log_hr = ln(1.29) = 0.254642; SE = (ln(1.52) - ln(1.09))/3.92 = (0.418710 - 0.086178)/3.92 = 0.084830. Positive = elevated mortality with short sleep. n = 88,282 UK Biobank adults with 2,973 deaths over an average 6.8 years; the spline model was fit on the full cohort, so I used the cohort N rather than any subgroup. Design prospective_cohort_objective (Axivity AX3 accelerometry, GGIR/HDCZA sleep detection) -> T4. RoB moderate: the authors note residual confounding, no light-at-night data, actigraphy is an indirect sleep measure, accelerometry collected ~5 years after baseline covariates, and possible reverse causation.

citation: Lim J, Dinges DF. A meta-analysis of the impact of short-term sleep deprivation on cognitive variables. Psychological Bulletin. 2010;136(3):375-389.
your_quote: Complex attention | Accuracy | −0.479** | 0.007 | 0.082 | −0.640 | −0.318 | 56.79 | 24 | 31.7 | Reaction time | −0.312** | 0.003 | 0.059 | −0.429 | −0.197 | 192.57 | 36 | 53.5 [Table 2, Combined Effect Sizes by Domain and Outcome Variable]
your_note: Full text obtained via PMC. Target construct 'complex_attention_reaction_time' maps to the Complex attention / Reaction time row of Table 2: g = -0.312, SE = 0.059 (as printed), 95% CI [-0.429, -0.197]. Consistency check: (-0.197 - (-0.429))/3.92 = 0.232/3.92 = 0.0592, matching the printed SE, so I used the paper's own SE. Negative = slower reaction time (worse) after short-term total sleep deprivation, already in the required sign convention (Lim & Dinges code all impairments negative). your_n is null: the meta-analysis reports k = 37 tests for this cell (Q = 192.57 on df = 36) but not a pooled participant count for the complex-attention reaction-time subset. RoB moderate: I2 = 53.5%, and the pooled primary studies mix within- and between-subject sleep-deprivation protocols of 24-48 h with heterogeneous test characteristics (the authors flag complex attention as their most heterogeneous category).

citation: Wilkins JT, Ning H, Berry J, Zhao L, Dyer AR, Lloyd-Jones DM. Lifetime risk and years lived free of total cardiovascular disease. JAMA. 2012;308(17):1795-1801.
target_unit: probability of any total CVD event (CHD, stroke, heart failure, other CVD death) from exact age 45 to age 95
your_quote: At an index age of 45 years, overall LTR estimates for tCVD through age 95 were 60.3% (95% CI, 59.3 to 61.2) for men, and 55.6% (95% CI, 54.5 to 56.7) for women.
your_note: Full text obtained via PMC. Value converted from percent to probability: 60.3% -> 0.603. SE = (0.612 - 0.593)/3.92 = 0.019/3.92 = 0.004847. n = 24,031 men at index age 45 (Table 2; 440,612 person-years, 8,472 CVD events); the frequently quoted 49,490 is men and women combined, so an extractor could enter that instead. Design life_table: modified Kaplan-Meier lifetime risk adjusted for the competing risk of non-CVD death, pooled across 5 community cohorts. RoB na: descriptive baseline-risk estimate, no exposure contrast.

citation: Fernandez-Mendoza J, He F, Vgontzas AN, Liao D, Bixler EO. Interplay of Objective Sleep Duration and Cardiovascular and Cerebrovascular Diseases on Cause-Specific Mortality. J Am Heart Assoc. 2019 Oct 15;8(20):e013043.
your_quote: When examined separately, the risks of all-cause mortality associated with CMRs and CBVD were 2.14 and 3.17 times higher, respectively, among those who slept <6 hours, whereas the risks were 1.38 and 2.34 times higher, respectively, among those who slept ≥6 hours (Table 2). ... | 2.14 (1.52–3.02)a
your_note: Full text obtained via PMC. Conversion: log_hr = ln(2.14) = 0.760806; SE = (ln(3.02) - ln(1.52))/3.92 = (1.105257 - 0.418710)/3.92 = 0.175139. SUSPECTED TARGET-SPECIFICATION PROBLEM, hence low confidence: the target frames habitual short sleep (<6 h, PSG-measured) as the exposure and 'all_cause_mortality_in_cardiometabolic_risk_subgroup' as the outcome, but 2.14 is the reverse decomposition - it is the HR for cardiometabolic risk factors (vs the CMR-free/CBVD-free reference group) ESTIMATED WITHIN the short-sleep stratum. The paper never reports a short-sleep-vs-normal-sleep HR within the CMR subgroup, so no number matches the target as literally written; 2.14 is the closest published quantity and is the one the paper headlines. Also note target_exposure_duration_days = 1 describes a single-night PSG measurement window, not an exposure duration. n = 1,654 adults aged <75 (512 deaths); the model uses the full cohort with a sleep-duration interaction, and the stratum-specific denominator is not reported (the <6 h group had 336 deaths at a 40.2% crude rate, implying roughly 836 people). RoB moderate: observational, single-night PSG exposure, residual confounding.

citation: Binks PG, Waters WF, Hurry M. Short-term total sleep deprivations does not selectively impair higher cortical functioning. Sleep. 1999;22(3):328-334.
your_quote: Table 2. Comparison of Control Subjects with Sleep Deprived Subjects (ANCOVAs) Covariate = Shipley Estimated IQ ... (n=32) (n=29) ... WAIS-R EST. IQ 102.5 (9.8) 106.1 (11.8) F(1,56) 0.46 p=.500
your_note: Full text obtained from the publisher's article page (Oxford Academic direct fetch was 403; the page text came through a web-search retrieval of the DOI landing page) and cross-checked against the first author's dissertation version of the same table. Binks reports no effect size, so I computed Hedges' g from the group means and SDs: control (n=32) M = 102.5, SD = 9.8; sleep-deprived (n=29) M = 106.1, SD = 11.8. Pooled SD = sqrt((31 x 9.8^2 + 28 x 11.8^2)/59) = sqrt(6875.96/59) = 10.7954. d = (106.1 - 102.5)/10.7954 = +0.333474. Hedges correction J = 1 - 3/(4 x 59 - 1) = 0.987234, so g = +0.329217. SE(d) = sqrt(61/928 + 0.333474^2/118) = sqrt(0.066675) = 0.258216; SE(g) = 0.258216 x 0.987234 = 0.254919. SIGN: POSITIVE because the sleep-deprived group scored 3.6 IQ points HIGHER than controls, i.e. the restricted condition was not worse; an extractor who assumed impairment and entered -0.33 would disagree with me on sign alone. Note the paper's own test is a Shipley-IQ-adjusted ANCOVA, F(1,56) = 0.46, p = .500, which is not identical to my unadjusted g. Design: subjects 'were then randomly assigned to either the control or sleep deprivation group', so this is a parallel randomized trial (T1), not a within-subject design - Lim & Dinges (2010) code Binks as 'WS' (within subjects), which is inconsistent with the paper. RoB some_concerns: no blinding, small groups, single testing session, no baseline cognitive measure other than the Shipley covariate.

citation: Baum KT, Desai A, Field J, Miller LE, Rausch J, Beebe DW. Sleep restriction worsens mood and emotion regulation in adolescents. J Child Psychol Psychiatry. 2014;55(2):180-190.
your_quote: Scores on the Oppositionality/Irritability (Z = −2.22, p = .03) and Emotion Regulation (Z = −2.40, p = .02) subscales were all significantly higher following the SR compared to HS, indicating greater oppositional behaviors, irritability, and emotional regulation problems.
your_note: Full text obtained via PMC. The paper reports NO effect size for this outcome, only Wilcoxon signed-rank statistics, so the requested cohens_d (within-subject d_z) had to be derived: d_z = Z/sqrt(N) = 2.40/sqrt(50) = 0.339411, signed negative because parent-rated emotion regulation problems were WORSE in the sleep-restricted condition. SE = d_z/Z = 1/sqrt(50) = 0.141421 (the alternative formula sqrt(1/N + d_z^2/(2N)) gives 0.145437). Confidence low because the Z-to-d conversion of a rank-based statistic is approximate and any other reasonable conversion (e.g. from medians/IQRs in Figure 4, or using r = Z/sqrt(N) then converting) would give a somewhat different number; this is a likely disagreement row. This is the PARENT-report Emotion Regulation subscale (Z = -2.40); the adolescent SELF-report Emotion Regulation value is Z = -2.71, which would give d_z = -0.383. n = 50 completers. Design: randomized counterbalanced crossover (6.5 h vs 10 h TIB for 5 nights each) conducted at home with actigraphy, so rct_crossover rather than lab_restriction_within_subject. RoB some_concerns: unblindable manipulation with subjective parent/teen ratings, though the authors included hyperactivity/impulsivity as a negative-control outcome.

citation: Rupp TL, Wesensten NJ, Bliese PD, Balkin TJ. Banking sleep: realization of benefits during subsequent sleep restriction and recovery. Sleep. 2009;32(3):311-321.
target_unit: additional PVT lapses per day of restriction, Habitual vs Extended
your_quote: RESTRICT X Group* | 0.40 | 0.17 | 273 | 2.35 | 0.01 [Table 5a, PVT lapses] ... During sleep restriction, the Habitual group showed a steeper slope of PVT performance deterioration for lapses compared to the Extended group (RESTRICT × Group).
your_note: Full text obtained via PMC. Value taken directly from the discontinuous growth model: the RESTRICT x Group interaction for PVT lapses is 0.40 (SE 0.17, t(273) = 2.35, p = 0.01), i.e. the Habitual group accumulated 0.40 more lapses per day of sleep restriction than the sleep-banked Extended group. Direction confirmed by the narrative ('the Habitual group showed a steeper slope ... compared to the Extended group'), so the positive sign matches target_unit 'Habitual vs Extended'. NOTE ON UNITS: target_scale is 'per_hour_beta' but this coefficient is per DAY of restriction (as target_unit itself says), not per hour of sleep; it is a slope, not a per-hour dose-response. Referent 7.09 h in the target is confirmed: 'Habitual TIB [mean (SD) hours = 7.09 (0.7)]'. n = 24 (12 per group), randomly assigned, so rct_parallel / T1. RoB some_concerns: n = 12 per group, no blinding possible, and the Extended group's baseline was taken after a week of extension, which the authors note complicates the recovery comparison.

citation: Chen P, Baylin A, Lee J, Dunietz GL, Cantoral A, Tellez Rojo MM, Peterson KE, Jansen EC. The association between sleep duration and sleep timing and insulin resistance among adolescents in Mexico City. J Adolesc Health. 2021 Jul;69(1):57-63.
target_unit: change in log HOMA-IR per +1 h later weekday sleep midpoint
your_quote: Later midpoints on weekdays and the weekend were associated with higher log HOMA-IR after adjusting for age, sex, and sleep duration (β= 0.0408, 95% CI −0.0049 to 0.087, P=0.08 and β=0.0486, 95% CI 0.0042 to 0.093, respectively).
your_note: Full text obtained via PMC. Value taken directly, no conversion: +0.0408 change in log HOMA-IR per +1 h later WEEKDAY sleep midpoint, adjusted for age, sex and sleep duration. SE = (0.087 - (-0.0049))/3.92 = 0.0919/3.92 = 0.023444. n = 384 Mexican adolescents. SUSPECTED TARGET-SPECIFICATION PROBLEM: target_exposure_type is 'social_jetlag', but the construct named (weekday sleep midpoint) is a different exposure, and the paper explicitly reports 'There were no associations between social jetlag and HOMA-IR, neither in unstratified nor sex-stratified analysis' - so a social-jetlag reading of this row has no matching number. I extracted the weekday-midpoint coefficient named in the construct. Other candidates that could cause disagreement: the weekend midpoint (0.0486, 0.0042 to 0.093) and the girls-only weekday midpoint (0.091, 0.027 to 0.16). Design cross_sectional (the authors state 'the cross-sectional design does not rule out the possibility of reverse causation'), hence TX; RoB moderate for unmeasured confounding (family history of diabetes, OSA) and reverse causation.

citation: Koyama AK, Cheng YJ, Brinks R, Xie H, Gregg EW, Hoyer A, Pavkov ME, Imperatore G. Trends in lifetime risk and years of potential life lost from diabetes in the United States, 1997-2018. PLoS One. 2022;17(5):e0268805.
target_unit: years of potential life lost due to diabetes, adult aged 20
your_quote: For example, during the earliest time period in 1997–1999, a person diagnosed with diabetes at age 20 was estimated to lose on average 8.9 (95% CI: 8.7–9.1) years of potential life due to diabetes, decreasing to an average of 6.2 (95% CI: 6.1–6.4) years in 2015–2018.
your_note: Full text obtained via PMC (PLOS One, open access). Value taken directly: YPLL due to diabetes for an adult diagnosed at age 20 in the most recent period, 2015-2018 = 6.2 years. SE = (6.4 - 6.1)/3.92 = 0.3/3.92 = 0.076531; note the interval is a Monte Carlo simulation interval (1,000 replications, 2.5th/97.5th percentiles) rather than an analytic CI, so treating it as a normal-theory CI is an approximation. n = 653,811 NHIS adults across all five survey periods. Design life_table: multistate difference-equation model with competing risks built on serial cross-sectional NHIS incidence and mortality. RoB na: descriptive model-based burden estimate, no exposure contrast.

citation: Fjell AM, Sorensen O, Wang Y, Amlien IK, Baare WFC, Bartres-Faz D, et al. No phenotypic or genotypic evidence for a link between sleep duration and brain atrophy. Nature Human Behaviour. 2023;7(11):2008-2022.
target_unit: hours of self-reported sleep at the volumetric/thickness optimum
your_quote: In contrast, cross-sectional analyses (51,295 observations) showed inverse U-shaped relationships, where a duration of 6.5 (95% confidence interval, (5.7, 7.3)) hours was associated with the thickest cortex and largest volumes relative to intracranial volume.
your_note: Full text obtained via PMC. Value taken directly: the meta-analytic sleep duration at maximum cortical thickness / relative volume = 6.5 h (95% CI 5.7, 7.3). SE = (7.3 - 5.7)/3.92 = 1.6/3.92 = 0.408163. n = 51,295 cross-sectional observations (not unique participants; the longitudinal arm is 8,153 MRIs from 3,893 adults). Important qualifier: 6.5 h is the ICV-ADJUSTED estimate; without controlling for intracranial volume the Results give 7.0 h (95% CI 6.3, 7.7) while the Discussion says 7.4 h for the same analysis - an internal inconsistency in the paper, so an extractor targeting the unadjusted optimum could enter either 7.0 or 7.4. Also note regional heterogeneity (hippocampus peaks at 6.3 h, cortical thickness 6.4-7.0 h). Design cross_sectional -> TX; RoB moderate because this is an associational optimum from cross-sectional data that the authors themselves say reflects mostly stable, early-developmental differences rather than effects of sleep.

citation: Scott AJ, Webb TL, Martyn-St James M, Rowse G, Weich S. Improving sleep quality leads to better mental health: A meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials. Sleep Med Rev. 2021 Dec;60:101556.
your_quote: Depression−0.63***−0.84 to −0.4381%322.03***617868 [Table 3, The effect of improving sleep on mental health outcomes: Outcome / g+ / 95% CI / I2 / Q / k / N] ... Improving sleep led to a significant medium-sized effect on composite mental health (g+ = −0.53), depression (g+ = −0.63), anxiety (g+ = −0.51), and rumination (g+ = −0.49)
your_note: Full text obtained via PMC. Depression outcome: g+ = -0.63, 95% CI -0.84 to -0.43, I2 = 81%, Q = 322.03, k = 61, N = 7,868. SE = (-0.43 - (-0.84))/3.92 = 0.41/3.92 = 0.104592. SIGN: Scott et al. already code negative as 'improving sleep reduced depression symptoms', which is equivalent to the control (poorer-sleep) arm having the worse outcome, so the reported -0.63 already satisfies the task's convention (negative = worse outcome under the shorter/poorer-sleep condition) and I did NOT flip it. n = 7,868 participants contributing to the depression estimate. Design meta_analysis_of_trials -> T1 (all included studies are RCTs that verifiably improved sleep quality). RoB high: the authors report that 'the majority of RCTs included in the present review were at high risk, or unclear risk of bias', I2 = 81%, and some evidence of publication bias; also the interventions are sleep-quality (mostly CBT-I) interventions rather than sleep-duration extension, which is a mismatch with target_exposure_type 'sleep_extension'.

citation: Moore SC, Patel AV, Matthews CE, Berrington de Gonzalez A, Park Y, Katki HA, Linet MS, Weiderpass E, Visvanathan K, Helzlsouer KJ, Thun M, Gapstur SM, Hartge P, Lee IM. Leisure time physical activity of moderate to vigorous intensity and mortality: a large pooled cohort analysis. PLoS Med. 2012;9(11):e1001335.
target_unit: years of life expectancy gained after age 40
your_quote: Levels at or just above the minimum level recommended by guidelines (7.5–14.9 MET-h/wk) were associated with even lower risks of mortality (HR = 0.68; 95% CI: 0.66–0.69) and higher life expectancies (3.4 y higher; 95% CI: 3.2–3.6).
your_note: Full text obtained via PMC (PLOS Medicine, open access). Value taken directly: 3.4 years of additional life expectancy after age 40 for 7.5-14.9 MET-h/wk of moderate-to-vigorous leisure-time physical activity versus the 0 MET-h/wk referent. SE = (3.6 - 3.2)/3.92 = 0.4/3.92 = 0.102041. n = 638,855 participants aged 40+ used for the life-expectancy analyses (82,315 deaths); the full pooled physical-activity analysis sample is 654,827, so an extractor could enter that instead. Design: pooled analysis of six prospective cohorts with self-reported physical activity, life expectancy derived from direct adjusted survival curves -> prospective_cohort_selfreport / T5 (life_table would also be arguable since the years-of-life metric comes from survival curves). RoB moderate: observational with self-reported exposure, significant between-study heterogeneity (p < 0.05 for all activity categories), residual confounding. This is a comparator (non-sleep) exposure.

citation: Smith MG, Wusk GC, Nasrini J, Baskin P, Dinges DF, Roma PG, Basner M. Effects of six weeks of chronic sleep restriction with weekend recovery on cognitive performance and wellbeing in high-performing adults. Sleep. 2021;44(8):zsab051.
target_unit: standardized beta per unit cumulative sleep debt
your_quote: There were some small to moderate effects of increasing sleep debt relative to pre-mission baseline, with decreases in accuracy across cognitive domains (standardized β = -0.121, p = 0.001), specifically on tests of spatial orientation (β = -0.289, p = 0.011) and vigilant attention (β = -0.688, p < 0.001), which were not restored by two nights of weekend recovery sleep.
your_note: Only the PubMed abstract was retrievable (Oxford Academic returned 403 for the Sleep full text and there is no PMC deposit). Value taken directly: standardized beta = -0.121 for accuracy across all cognitive domains per unit of cumulative sleep debt; negative = worse accuracy with accumulating sleep debt, consistent with the required sign convention. SE derived from the p-value: for two-sided p = 0.001 the normal deviate is z = 3.290527, so SE = 0.121/3.290527 = 0.036772. Confidence low for two reasons: (1) p is reported rounded to '0.001', so the derived SE could be off by a fair margin, and with n = 15 a t-based rather than normal-based deviate would be more appropriate but the degrees of freedom of the mixed model are not in the abstract; (2) TARGET-SPECIFICATION MISMATCH - target_scale says hedges_g but the quantity is a standardized regression coefficient per unit sleep debt (target_unit concedes this), and target_exposure_dose_h = 8 with target_exposure_referent_h = 5 appears inverted relative to the protocol, in which 5 h was the weekday restriction and 8 h the weekend recovery opportunity. n = 15 high-performing adults confined in groups of 4. Design: single-arm 6-week within-subject chronic restriction with repeated measures, no randomized control -> lab_restriction_within_subject / T1. RoB moderate: no control group, protocol breaches (occasional daytime napping), caffeine access, and evening testing near the circadian peak.
